title: Capitals of the World
summary: What makes a city a capital, how countries choose or build their capital cities, and examples from around the world, including Riyadh as the capital of Saudi Arabia.
poll: A country's capital city should always be its largest city.

versions.title: Capitals of the World
versions.text:
Each country has one city. It is a capital.

Leaders work there. They make laws. They meet there. They rule from there.

Is this city the biggest? Not always. Some lands pick a small town.

One land has a capital. Its name is Riyadh. The city is big. It grows each year.

Many men live there. Many women live there too. They work there each day.

Each land has its own capital. No two are the same. Some sit near the sea.

Some are old. Some are new. A few were made just for this.

This city is key. It sits at the heart of a land. It is a land's rule.

versions.title: Capitals of the World
versions.text:
Nearly every country has one city that serves as its capital. This is the place where the main work of government happens. What makes a city a capital, and how is it picked?

A capital is usually the official seat of a country's leaders. Big choices for the whole land get made there.

A capital is not always a country's biggest city. Some lands keep their capital in an old, historic city. Others pick a new spot, often for plain, practical reasons.

Some capitals were planned and built from scratch. Washington, D.C. and Canberra were both planned cities. They were built to be fair, central capitals.

Saudi Arabia's capital, Riyadh, is located near the middle of the land. Riyadh is the official home of the Saudi government. It has grown fast into one of the biggest cities in the region.

Why build a brand-new capital at all? A spot near the middle can feel fair to every region of a big land.

At other times, a historic capital just keeps the role it has held for years. It ties a land's rule to its past.

Across the world, capitals serve one goal. Each stays the official hub of a country's rule.

A capital is typically the official seat of a country's leaders and lawmakers. Consequential decisions for the whole wide land are made there.

versions.title: Capitals of the World
versions.text:
Nearly every country designates one city as its capital, the administrative center for a nation's main work of government. What makes a city a capital, and how is it chosen?

A capital is usually the official seat of government, housing a country's leaders and administrative offices. Big decisions for the whole land are made there. A capital often carries symbolic weight too, standing for the unity and shared identity of a whole country.

A capital is not always a country's largest city. Some nations keep their capital in an old, historic city. Others pick a different spot, often for plain administrative reasons.

Some nations have chosen to relocate their capital entirely. Brazil relocated its capital from Rio de Janeiro to the new city of Brasilia in 1960. Nigeria later also relocated its capital from Lagos to the planned city of Abuja.

Building a brand-new capital needs huge infrastructure. Roads, homes, offices, and water systems must rise almost overnight to support a city's new administrative role from the very start.

Saudi Arabia's capital, Riyadh, is located near the middle of the country and serves as the official, administrative home of both the Saudi government and the royal family. Riyadh has grown fast, backed by infrastructure built to match its growing role.

Why relocate or designate a whole new capital? A central spot can feel fair to every region of a sprawling country, and a new capital can also stand as a symbolic fresh start for the whole nation moving forward.

Across the world, capitals serve the same goal, whether old or newly designated: each stays the administrative and symbolic hub of a nation's rule. Some sit on a busy coast, some sit deep inland, and some sit high in cool hills, chosen for reasons as different as the countries themselves.

keyWords.definition: representing something important beyond its ordinary, practical meaning
keyWords.example: Planting a tree on the school's first day became a symbolic tradition.

keyWords.definition: the basic systems a place needs, such as roads, buildings, and utilities
keyWords.example: The town built new infrastructure, including roads and a water system, before the houses were built.

keyWords.definition: to officially choose or name something for a particular purpose
keyWords.example: The city council voted to designate the old building as a museum.

questions.stem: Which statement best summarizes the article?
options: A capital is both the seat of government and a symbol of national identity
Every capital is always the largest and oldest city around
Capitals have only existed since fairly modern times began
Riyadh is described as the single largest city on Earth
questions.why: The article shows capitals serve both an administrative and a symbolic role, and that countries choose or build them for varied practical reasons.

wrong.B: The article explains that capitals are not always the largest or oldest city.
wrong.C: The article discusses historic capitals as well as modern ones.
wrong.D: Riyadh is described as large and modern, but not as the largest city in the world.

questions.stem: What does the article say happened to Brazil's capital in 1960?
options: It was moved all the way across the ocean to Lisbon
It was relocated from Rio de Janeiro to the new city of Brasilia
It stayed fixed in Rio de Janeiro for good, permanently
It slowly became a small, uninhabited island nearby
questions.why: The article says Brazil relocated its capital from Rio de Janeiro to the newly built city of Brasilia in 1960.

wrong.A: Lisbon is in Portugal, not mentioned as Brazil's capital.
wrong.C: The article says the capital moved away from Rio de Janeiro.
wrong.D: The article does not describe Brasilia as an island.

questions.stem: Which country relocated its capital from Lagos to Abuja, according to the article?
options: The large country of Brazil in South America
The country of Australia, far away in the Pacific
Nigeria
The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia on the Arabian Peninsula
questions.why: The article says Nigeria relocated its capital from Lagos to the planned city of Abuja.

wrong.A: Brazil relocated its capital to Brasilia, not Abuja.
wrong.B: Australia's planned capital is Canberra, not Abuja.
wrong.D: Saudi Arabia's capital is Riyadh, not Abuja.

questions.stem: The article says a capital often carries 'symbolic' weight. What does symbolic mean here?
options: Made only of symbols instead of real buildings
Related only to numbers and simple mathematics
Having absolutely no meaning or purpose at all
Representing something larger, like a country's identity
questions.why: Symbolic here means representing something larger, such as a country's unity or identity, beyond the capital's practical role.

wrong.A: A symbolic city is still a real city with real buildings.
wrong.B: Mathematics is unrelated to this meaning.
wrong.C: Symbolic weight means having meaning, not lacking it.

questions.stem: Why does building a brand-new capital require so much infrastructure?
options: Because brand-new capitals are never allowed to have any roads
Because a new city needs buildings, roads, and utilities built from scratch
Because infrastructure only matters inside much older cities
Because new capitals always stay smaller than tiny villages
questions.why: A brand-new capital needs infrastructure like buildings, roads, housing, and utilities built from the ground up to support its new role.

wrong.A: New capitals do have roads; the article even mentions roadways as part of their infrastructure.
wrong.C: The article describes infrastructure as necessary for new capitals.
wrong.D: New capitals like Brasilia and Abuja are described as growing large cities, not small villages.

questions.stem: Based on the article, why might a country designate a new, central capital instead of an older coastal one?
options: A central location can feel more fair to different regions of the country
Because coastal cities are never legally allowed to be capitals
Because every new capital must be built out on an island
Because older capital cities no longer have any leaders
questions.why: The article explains that a centrally positioned location can feel fairer and more balanced to different regions of a large country than a coastal one.

wrong.B: The article does not say coastal cities can never be capitals.
wrong.C: New capitals like Brasilia and Abuja are not described as islands.
wrong.D: Older capitals still have leaders; countries just chose to move the capital.

questions.stem: According to the article, what is one reason a newly designated capital might also serve a symbolic purpose?
options: It stops a country from ever having any laws at all
It removes the need for a country to build any offices
It makes a country's older cities vanish completely overnight
It can represent a fresh start or a more unified national identity
questions.why: The article explains that a newly designated capital can symbolize a fresh start or a more unified national identity for the country.

wrong.A: The article does not say laws disappear with a new capital.
wrong.B: New capitals still need government buildings, as the article explains.
wrong.C: The article does not say older cities disappear.

questions.stem: How do the examples of Brasilia and Abuja support the article's larger point about capitals?
options: They prove that every single capital must sit along a coast
They explain the best methods for growing crops in a desert
They show real cases of countries relocating a capital for practical and symbolic reasons
They describe ancient trade routes used many centuries ago
questions.why: Brasilia and Abuja serve as concrete, real-world examples supporting the article's point that countries sometimes relocate capitals for administrative and symbolic reasons.

wrong.A: Brasilia and Abuja are examples of inland, planned capitals, not coastal ones.
wrong.B: Growing crops is not discussed in the article.
wrong.D: Ancient trade routes are not discussed in this article.

HIGH.prompt: Some countries, like Brazil and Nigeria, chose to relocate their capital to a brand-new, planned city. Do you think this is usually a good decision? Support your position with evidence from the article.
checklist: I supported it with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how my evidence supports my position.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I think relocating a capital to a new, planned city can be a good decision for a large, diverse country. The article explains that Brazil relocated its capital from Rio de Janeiro to Brasilia, and Nigeria relocated its capital from Lagos to Abuja, both moving toward more centrally positioned locations. A central, newly designated capital can feel fairer to different regions and can also carry symbolic weight, representing a fresh start for the whole nation, even though building the necessary infrastructure takes enormous effort.
